frameworks.name: SWOT Analysis
frameworks.definition: A structured framework that evaluates an entity's internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats, usually presented as a 2x2 matrix.
frameworks.purpose: To match internal capabilities with the external environment so that strategic options (SO/WO/ST/WT strategies) can be identified and prioritised.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Strategy formulation and review; investment or expansion appraisal context-setting; competitor and own-position assessment; turnaround diagnosis.
frameworks.required_inputs: Reliable internal performance data (financials, operations, capabilities); market and industry information; competitor intelligence.
frameworks.limitations: A static snapshot — it does not show change over time; highly subjective unless evidenced; produces lists, not priorities, unless paired with weighting or quantification.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Listing factors with no analysis or 'so what' implication; confusing internal factors with external ones (e.g. putting competitor actions under Weaknesses); treating every point as equally important.
frameworks.example: A Karachi textile exporter: Strength — established EU buyer relationships; Weakness — dependence on grid electricity with load-shedding exposure; Opportunity — GSP+ preferential access; Threat — lower-cost regional competitors. Implication: prioritise captive power investment (WO strategy).
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: PESTEL Analysis
frameworks.definition: A macro-environment scanning framework covering Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal factors affecting an organisation.
frameworks.purpose: To identify external drivers of change that create opportunities or threats, feeding into strategy, forecasting and risk assessment.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Market entry or expansion analysis; long-range planning; risk identification; setting assumptions for budgets and valuations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Country/sector data: policy and regulatory outlook, economic indicators, demographic and social trends, technology trends, environmental regulation, legal changes.
frameworks.limitations: Factors overlap and interact; easy to produce long unfocused lists; needs regular updating in volatile environments.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Treating factors as independent; listing generic factors with no link to the specific business; failing to convert findings into opportunities/threats.
frameworks.example: For a Pakistani FMCG entrant: P — sales tax documentation drive; E — rupee volatility raising import costs; S — urbanisation boosting packaged-food demand; T — e-commerce growth; E — plastic packaging regulation; L — Companies Act compliance costs.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Porter's Five Forces Model
frameworks.definition: An industry-analysis framework assessing five competitive forces: threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat of substitute products or services, and intensity of competitive rivalry.
frameworks.purpose: To judge the structural attractiveness and profit potential of an industry and identify where competitive pressure comes from.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Industry selection and entry decisions; competitor benchmarking; explaining margin differences between industries; acquisition target screening.
frameworks.required_inputs: Industry structure data: concentration, entry barriers, switching costs, supplier/buyer concentration, substitute availability.
frameworks.limitations: Static and industry-level — less useful for fast-changing or platform markets; assumes clear industry boundaries; underplays complementors and regulation.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Describing the industry instead of analysing each force's strength; ignoring the interaction between forces; no conclusion on overall attractiveness.
frameworks.example: Pakistani cement: high entry barriers (capital, limestone reserves) weaken entrant threat; rivalry is intense in the North zone, depressing margins despite barriers.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Product Life Cycle Model
frameworks.definition: A model describing the stages a product passes through — introduction, growth, maturity and decline — and the typical sales, profit, cash flow and strategy implications of each stage.
frameworks.purpose: To align marketing, operations and financial strategy (pricing, promotion, capacity, cash management) with the product's stage.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Product strategy and pricing decisions; portfolio reviews; forecasting sales and cash flows; deciding on product withdrawal or relaunch.
frameworks.required_inputs: Product sales history, market growth rates, competitor product ages, cost and margin by product.
frameworks.limitations: Stages are hard to identify in real time; not all products follow the pattern (fads, revivals); length of stages varies widely.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Forcing every product into a stage without evidence; ignoring that strategy can extend or reshape the cycle.
frameworks.example: A mature detergent brand shows flat sales and price-based competition — harvest cash, cut promotion, consider a relaunch or line extension rather than capacity expansion.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Boston Consulting Group Matrix
frameworks.definition: A portfolio matrix plotting business units or products on relative market share (x-axis) against market growth rate (y-axis), giving four quadrants: Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks and Dogs.
frameworks.purpose: To guide resource allocation across a portfolio — which units to invest in, harvest, divest or selectively support.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Multi-product or multi-division companies; capital allocation and divestment decisions; acquisition portfolio fit.
frameworks.required_inputs: Revenue by unit/product, market size and growth rates, largest competitor's share (for relative share).
frameworks.limitations: Only two dimensions — ignores synergies, brand value and risk; market definition drives the answer; high share does not always mean high profit.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Defining the market so the answer is predetermined; recommending divestment of every Dog without checking cash or strategic value; ignoring interdependencies between units.
frameworks.example: A conglomerate: its cement unit is a Cash Cow funding the Question Mark fintech venture; the loss-making textile Dog with no turnaround plan is a divestment candidate.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Tucker's 5-Question Ethical Model
frameworks.definition: An ethical decision-making model presented by Graham Tucker asking five questions: 1) Is it profitable? 2) Is it legal? 3) Is it fair? 4) Is it right? 5) Is it sustainable development / consistent with the organisation's values?
frameworks.purpose: To provide a quick, structured ethical screen for business decisions, moving from commercial to moral tests.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Ethical dilemmas in cases: aggressive accounting, supplier treatment, environmental trade-offs, staff decisions.
frameworks.required_inputs: The facts of the decision, relevant law and regulation, stakeholder impacts, the organisation's stated values.
frameworks.limitations: Questions can conflict (profitable but unfair); 'right' and 'fair' remain judgemental; gives a verdict, not a resolution process.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Stopping at 'is it legal' — legality is necessary but not sufficient; answering the questions with assertion rather than evidence.
frameworks.example: Delaying supplier payments to flatter year-end cash: profitable (yes), legal (borderline), fair (no) — the model flags it at question 3 even if technically legal.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: American Accounting Association 7-Step Ethical Model
frameworks.definition: A seven-step ethical decision process: 1) determine the facts, 2) define the ethical issues, 3) identify major principles, rules and values, 4) specify the alternatives, 5) compare values and alternatives, 6) assess the consequences, 7) make the decision.
frameworks.purpose: To work through an ethical dilemma methodically, making the values and trade-offs explicit before deciding.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Complex ethical cases with competing stakeholder claims; professional conduct dilemmas; whistleblowing and reporting decisions.
frameworks.required_inputs: Verified facts, applicable codes and principles (e.g. ICAP Code of Ethics concepts), stakeholder map, feasible alternatives.
frameworks.limitations: Time-consuming; steps 3 and 5 depend heavily on personal/professional judgement; does not guarantee consensus.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Skipping fact-finding and jumping to judgement; listing only two extreme alternatives; ignoring long-term consequences in step 6.
frameworks.example: A finance manager pressured to capitalise operating expenses: facts established (step 1), issue defined as integrity vs loyalty (step 2), alternatives from refusal to escalation to the audit committee (step 4), decision with documented rationale (step 7).
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Value Chain Analysis
frameworks.definition: Porter's value chain disaggregates a firm into primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities (infrastructure, HR, technology development, procurement) to locate where value and margin are created.
frameworks.purpose: To identify sources of cost advantage or differentiation and to target improvement efforts where they create the most value.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Operational inefficiency diagnosis; outsourcing and make-or-buy analysis; competitor cost comparison; digital transformation scoping.
frameworks.required_inputs: Activity-level cost data, process maps, competitor benchmarks, customer value perceptions.
frameworks.limitations: Activity costs are often estimated, not observed; static view of a dynamic chain; less suited to pure service or platform businesses without adaptation.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Analysing activities in isolation from linkages between them; confusing cost cutting in one activity with value creation overall.
frameworks.example: A pharma distributor finds 60% of order-processing cost sits in manual documentation (support activity) — automation there improves margin more than squeezing transport rates.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Stakeholder Analysis
frameworks.definition: A framework for identifying stakeholders, assessing their power and interest (power-interest grid), and planning engagement: manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, or monitor.
frameworks.purpose: To anticipate resistance and support, and to design communication and negotiation strategies for a decision or change.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Mergers, restructuring, financing and dividend decisions; regulatory or community-sensitive projects; family business succession.
frameworks.required_inputs: Stakeholder list, assessment of each party's influence and interest, their objectives and likely positions.
frameworks.limitations: Positions shift over time; power is hard to measure; the grid oversimplifies coalitions between stakeholders.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Omitting less visible stakeholders (regulators, lenders' covenants, key staff); treating the analysis as one-off rather than updating it.
frameworks.example: A rights issue: existing shareholders (high power, high interest) must be managed closely on dilution and TERP; lenders (high power) need covenant reassurance.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Business Model Canvas
frameworks.definition: A nine-block visual framework describing how an organisation creates and captures value: customer segments, value propositions, channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partnerships and cost structure.
frameworks.purpose: To give a complete, one-page picture of how a business works, exposing gaps, risks and assumptions in the model.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Start-up and new-venture analysis; business model change (e.g. product to subscription); competitor model comparison.
frameworks.required_inputs: Understanding of customers, revenues, costs, partners and resources — often from management interviews and financials.
frameworks.limitations: Descriptive, not analytical — it maps the model but does not test viability; needs pairing with financial analysis.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Filling blocks with aspirations instead of evidence; ignoring the cost structure and revenue stream blocks where finance insight matters most.
frameworks.example: A cloud-kitchen start-up: value proposition is 30-minute delivery; key risk sits in the cost structure block (rider costs) and revenue stream block (commission dependence on aggregators).
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Root Cause Analysis
frameworks.definition: A structured technique (5 Whys, fishbone/Ishikawa diagram) for tracing an observed problem back through causal chains to its underlying root causes, separating symptoms from causes.
frameworks.purpose: To ensure recommendations fix causes rather than symptoms, so problems do not recur.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Declining performance, quality failures, cost overruns, repeated variances, customer complaints.
frameworks.required_inputs: Problem statement with evidence, process data, operator/management input, timeline of events.
frameworks.limitations: Causal chains can branch and loop; stopping too early gives a proximate cause, not the root; needs honest input.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Stopping at the first plausible cause; blaming people instead of processes; recommending solutions before causes are established.
frameworks.example: Falling gross margin traced: symptom — margin down 4pp; proximate — higher material prices; root — purchasing moved to spot buying after a supplier dispute, losing contract discounts.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Problem Tree / Issue Tree
frameworks.definition: A MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) decomposition of a central problem into causes (roots) and effects (branches), or of a key question into sub-questions.
frameworks.purpose: To structure messy problems so each part can be analysed and evidenced separately, then recombined into a recommendation.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Case analysis structuring; exam answers needing clear logic; complex multi-issue scenarios.
frameworks.required_inputs: A crisp problem statement or key question; hypotheses about drivers; data to test each branch.
frameworks.limitations: Quality depends on the initial structuring — a bad tree misdirects effort; branches may interact, breaking MECE purity.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Branches that overlap or miss major drivers; confusing causes with effects; never pruning branches the evidence rules out.
frameworks.example: Declining profitability decomposed into revenue branches (volume, price, mix) and cost branches (material, labour, overhead) — each tested against the numbers.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Cost-Benefit Analysis
frameworks.definition: A decision framework that lists all relevant costs and benefits of an option, quantifies them in money terms where possible, discounts future flows, and compares net benefit across alternatives.
frameworks.purpose: To give a disciplined, comparable economic basis for choosing between options, including non-obvious costs and benefits.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Project and policy choices; make-or-buy; system investments; any decision with mixed financial and non-financial effects.
frameworks.required_inputs: Relevant (incremental) costs and benefits, timing of cash flows, discount rate, key assumptions.
frameworks.limitations: Intangibles are hard to quantify and easy to manipulate; results are assumption-driven — sensitivity analysis is essential.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Including sunk costs; omitting opportunity costs; using nominal flows with a real discount rate (or vice versa); presenting a single-point answer without sensitivity.
frameworks.example: ERP implementation: licence and training costs vs labour savings, error reduction and faster close — NPV of net benefits positive only if headcount savings materialise (sensitivity on the key benefit).
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: ISO 31000 Risk Management
frameworks.definition: The ISO 31000 risk management approach: principles, framework and process — establishing scope, context and criteria; risk assessment (identification, analysis, evaluation); risk treatment; monitoring and review; communication and consultation; recording and reporting.
frameworks.purpose: To embed a systematic, organisation-wide process for managing uncertainty's effect on objectives.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Enterprise risk reviews; assessing business and financial risks; designing risk responses and controls.
frameworks.required_inputs: Objectives and risk criteria, risk identification workshops/data, likelihood and impact assessments, existing controls.
frameworks.limitations: A process standard, not a quantification method — needs pairing with measurement techniques; can become bureaucratic without ownership.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Producing a risk register that is never reviewed; confusing risk identification with risk measurement; no link between risks and strategy.
frameworks.example: An exporter applies the process: identifies FX exposure (identification), measures it (analysis), compares against tolerance (evaluation), and hedges 70% of exposures (treatment).
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Implementation Planning
frameworks.definition: A framework for turning a recommendation into action: objectives, sequenced actions, owners (RACI), milestones and deadlines, resources, risks and contingencies, and monitoring measures.
frameworks.purpose: To make recommendations credible and executable by showing exactly how, by whom and by when they will be delivered.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Recommendation sections of case answers; turnaround and change programmes; post-acquisition integration.
frameworks.required_inputs: The agreed recommendation, resource constraints, stakeholder positions, key dependencies.
frameworks.limitations: Plans assume stability — need review triggers; detail must match the decision's scale.
frameworks.common_mistakes: A recommendation with no implementation steps; ignoring change-management and communication; no contingency for the main risks.
frameworks.example: Working-capital turnaround plan: week 1–2 renegotiate supplier terms (owner: CFO), month 1–3 tighten credit control (owner: sales), monthly CCC reporting to the board.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Ratio Analysis
frameworks.definition: Analysis of financial statements through profitability, liquidity, efficiency (activity), gearing and investor ratios, interpreted via trend (time series) and peer/industry comparison.
frameworks.purpose: To diagnose financial performance, position and risk, and to flag areas needing deeper investigation.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Performance reviews; credit and investment appraisal; early-warning and turnaround analysis; exam financial-analysis questions.
frameworks.required_inputs: At least 2–3 years of financial statements, industry benchmarks, notes on accounting policies and one-offs.
frameworks.limitations: Ratios describe, they do not explain — they need narrative and investigation; distorted by accounting choices, inflation and window-dressing.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Computing ratios with no interpretation; comparing without adjusting for different year-ends or policies; ignoring the cash flow statement.
frameworks.example: Receivable days rising from 45 to 78 while revenue is flat signals collection problems or channel-stuffing — the ratio flags it, investigation explains it.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Trend and Common-Size Analysis
frameworks.definition: Horizontal analysis (year-on-year change and index numbers) and vertical/common-size analysis (each line as a percentage of revenue or total assets) to reveal structural shifts in financial statements.
frameworks.purpose: To spot emerging patterns — margin drift, cost creep, balance-sheet structure changes — before they become crises.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Multi-year performance reviews; budget variance context; forensic-style anomaly spotting.
frameworks.required_inputs: 3–5 years of financial statements on a consistent basis; notes on restatements and policy changes.
frameworks.limitations: Needs consistent accounting bases; inflation distorts long series; a trend is not a cause.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Reading a one-year movement as a trend; not rebasing for acquisitions or disposals; ignoring base effects on percentages.
frameworks.example: Common-sizing shows distribution costs rising from 8% to 13% of revenue over four years while gross margin is stable — the problem is below gross profit.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Variance Analysis
frameworks.definition: Comparison of actual results against budget/standard, decomposing differences into price and usage/efficiency components for materials, labour and overheads, plus sales volume and price variances; distinguishing planning from operational variances.
frameworks.purpose: To assign responsibility for deviations, trigger corrective action, and improve future budgets and standards.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Budgetary control reviews; manufacturing performance analysis; investigating profit shortfalls.
frameworks.required_inputs: Budgets/standards, actual quantities, prices and costs; separation of controllable vs uncontrollable factors.
frameworks.limitations: Standards may be outdated; variances interact (cheap material causing adverse labour efficiency); investigation has a cost.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Investigating every variance instead of material/exceptional ones; treating favourable variances as automatically good; ignoring planning variances caused by unrealistic budgets.
frameworks.example: Adverse material price variance of Rs 2.4m traced to spot buying after a supplier dispute — an operational variance, controllable by procurement, not by production.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Benchmarking
frameworks.definition: Systematic comparison of processes, costs or performance against internal units, competitors or best-in-class firms (internal, competitive, functional and generic benchmarking).
frameworks.purpose: To set realistic improvement targets and identify transferable best practices.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Cost reduction programmes; service-level improvement; justifying efficiency assumptions in budgets and valuations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Comparable metrics, peer data (published accounts, industry studies), process understanding.
frameworks.limitations: Like-for-like comparison is hard (scale, mix, accounting); best practice may not transfer; data availability.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Benchmarking the metric without understanding the process behind it; using incomparable peers; treating the benchmark as the target without a path to reach it.
frameworks.example: A distributor's 68-day cash conversion cycle vs an industry median of 41 days sets a quantified working-capital improvement target.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Breakeven and CVP Analysis
frameworks.definition: Cost-volume-profit analysis relating fixed and variable costs, contribution per unit and selling price: breakeven point, margin of safety, target-profit volumes, and sensitivity to price/cost changes.
frameworks.purpose: To quantify the volume and price needed for viability and to stress-test profit plans.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: New product or venture appraisal; pricing decisions; operational gearing assessment; shutdown vs continue choices.
frameworks.required_inputs: Selling price, variable cost per unit, total fixed costs, sales mix for multi-product cases.
frameworks.limitations: Assumes linearity and constant mix and prices; single-period and static; weak for highly stepped or joint costs.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using accounting profit instead of contribution; ignoring stepped fixed costs near capacity; applying single-product breakeven to a multi-product mix.
frameworks.example: Fixed costs Rs 12m, contribution Rs 400/unit → breakeven 30,000 units; at forecast 36,000 units the margin of safety is 16.7% — thin, so price sensitivity matters.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Contribution and Marginal Costing Analysis
frameworks.definition: Analysis based on contribution (sales minus variable costs): contribution per unit, contribution margin ratio, and ranking of products or orders by contribution per unit of limiting factor.
frameworks.purpose: To support short-term decisions — product emphasis, order acceptance, pricing floors — where fixed costs are sunk.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Special orders, product mix, discontinuation reviews, pricing in spare-capacity situations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Variable cost per unit (or per order), selling prices, limiting factor quantities, avoidable fixed costs.
frameworks.limitations: Short-term only — fixed costs matter in the long run; assumes variable costs are truly variable; ignores strategic and qualitative factors.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using full cost for short-term decisions; forgetting opportunity cost of the limiting factor; assuming spare capacity exists.
frameworks.example: Two products compete for machine hours: rank by contribution per machine hour, not per unit — the lower-margin product wins if it uses far fewer hours.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Capacity Utilisation Analysis
frameworks.definition: Analysis of practical capacity vs actual output: utilisation rates, bottleneck identification, cost of idle capacity, and the economics of expansion or rationalisation.
frameworks.purpose: To link operational capacity decisions to financial outcomes — when to expand, outsource, or cut capacity.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Expansion appraisals; bottleneck management; overhead absorption reviews; shutdown decisions.
frameworks.required_inputs: Practical/normal capacity, actual output, fixed cost structure, demand forecasts, expansion cost and lead time.
frameworks.limitations: Capacity definitions vary (theoretical vs practical); demand forecasts drive the conclusion; lumpy expansion creates step changes.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using theoretical maximum capacity; ignoring lead times; expanding for peak demand that is temporary.
frameworks.example: A plant at 92% utilisation with 8% annual demand growth hits constraint in year 2 — expansion NPV must weigh the cost of idle capacity against lost sales.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Working Capital Management
frameworks.definition: Management of the cash conversion cycle — inventory days + receivable days − payable days — through credit, inventory and payment policies, balancing liquidity against profitability.
frameworks.purpose: To free cash tied up in operations, reduce financing needs and avoid liquidity crises without damaging sales or supply.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Cash crises; rapid growth funding; credit policy reviews; pre-acquisition liquidity assessment.
frameworks.required_inputs: Receivable, inventory and payable days; credit terms; overdraft and financing costs; sales and purchase forecasts.
frameworks.limitations: Aggressive tightening can lose sales or suppliers; ratios are period-end snapshots; seasonal businesses need averages.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Cutting inventory below service-level needs; stretching payables until supply is disrupted; confusing profit with cash.
frameworks.example: Cutting receivable days from 75 to 55 on Rs 1.2bn sales releases Rs 65.8m of cash — but only if credit control does not lose key customers.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: KPI Design and Review
frameworks.definition: Selection and monitoring of key performance indicators — financial and non-financial, leading and lagging — that are specific, measurable and linked to objectives and accountability.
frameworks.purpose: To translate strategy into measurable targets and to give early warning of drift.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Performance management design; balanced performance reviews; monitoring turnaround or project delivery.
frameworks.required_inputs: Strategic objectives, data availability, baselines and targets, owners for each measure.
frameworks.limitations: What gets measured gets managed — gaming risk; too many KPIs dilute focus; lagging KPIs report history.
frameworks.common_mistakes: KPIs with no owner or target; vanity metrics; changing definitions period to period.
frameworks.example: A retailer tracks like-for-like sales growth (lagging), stock-out rate (leading) and staff turnover — each with an owner and monthly review.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Time Value of Money
frameworks.definition: The principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future: present value, future value, annuities and perpetuities, discounted at an appropriate rate.
frameworks.purpose: To put cash flows occurring at different times on a comparable basis — the foundation of all discounted appraisal.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Investment appraisal; valuation; lease vs buy; loan and bond calculations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Cash flow amounts and timing, discount rate, compounding frequency.
frameworks.limitations: Results hinge on the discount rate; assumes cash flows are known and reinvestment at the discount rate (for IRR, at the IRR).
frameworks.common_mistakes: Mixing nominal and real rates/flows; discounting accounting profit instead of cash flow; ignoring timing within the year.
frameworks.example: Rs 10m receivable in 3 years at 12% is worth Rs 7.12m today — any investment costing more than that to secure it destroys value.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Relevant Costing
frameworks.definition: Decision costing based on future, incremental cash flows: include only costs and revenues that change with the decision; exclude sunk and committed costs; include opportunity costs.
frameworks.purpose: To prevent irrelevant (sunk, allocated, committed) costs from distorting short-term decisions.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Special orders, make-or-buy, discontinuation, further processing, shutdown decisions.
frameworks.required_inputs: Incremental cash costs and revenues, opportunity costs of constrained resources, avoidable fixed costs.
frameworks.limitations: Short-term lens — repeated 'irrelevant' fixed costs eventually become relevant; qualitative factors still matter.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Including sunk costs or allocated overheads; forgetting opportunity cost; treating all fixed costs as irrelevant even when avoidable.
frameworks.example: A special order priced at Rs 850/unit with incremental cost Rs 620/unit and no capacity constraint adds Rs 230/unit — the Rs 200/unit absorbed fixed overhead is irrelevant.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Make-or-Buy Decision Framework
frameworks.definition: A structured comparison of in-house production vs outsourcing: relevant cost comparison, capacity and quality effects, strategic and supply-risk factors, then a quantified recommendation.
frameworks.purpose: To decide the lowest-risk, lowest-relevant-cost sourcing route without damaging capability or quality.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Component sourcing, service outsourcing (IT, logistics), vertical integration reviews.
frameworks.required_inputs: Relevant in-house cost (variable + avoidable fixed + opportunity cost), supplier quotes, quality and lead-time data, capacity position.
frameworks.limitations: Quotes may exclude transition costs; quality and reliability are hard to price; strategic capability loss is qualitative.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Comparing full cost instead of relevant cost; ignoring freed-capacity opportunity; no contract-risk assessment of the supplier.
frameworks.example: In-house relevant cost Rs 410/unit vs supplier Rs 385/unit, but freed capacity can generate Rs 60/unit contribution elsewhere — making is cheaper on a relevant-cost basis.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Special Order Pricing
frameworks.definition: Pricing logic for one-off orders: accept if incremental revenue exceeds incremental cost plus any opportunity cost, subject to capacity, legal and customer-relationship constraints.
frameworks.purpose: To set a defensible price floor for non-standard orders and avoid loss-making acceptance.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Export enquiries, bulk one-off orders, spare-capacity utilisation.
frameworks.required_inputs: Incremental cost per unit, opportunity cost of capacity used, order size, strategic/customer implications.
frameworks.limitations: Short-term view; repeated 'special' orders become normal business; price discrimination may leak to regular customers.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Accepting at a price below incremental cost to 'keep staff busy'; ignoring the reaction of existing customers to a lower price.
frameworks.example: Spare capacity of 5,000 units; incremental cost Rs 620; any price above Rs 620 plus delivery cost contributes — but check the regular customer's reaction first.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Product Mix Optimisation
frameworks.definition: Ranking products by contribution per unit of the limiting factor and allocating the scarce resource to the highest-ranked products until demand or capacity is exhausted.
frameworks.purpose: To maximise total contribution when a single scarce resource constrains output.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Scarce machine hours, labour hours or material; sales mix decisions; bottleneck scheduling.
frameworks.required_inputs: Contribution per unit, limiting-factor usage per unit, available limiting factor, maximum demand per product.
frameworks.limitations: Single limiting factor only — multiple constraints need linear programming; assumes fixed prices and costs; ignores strategic products.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Ranking by contribution per unit instead of per limiting factor; ignoring demand limits (producing more than can be sold).
frameworks.example: Machine hours are scarce: product A gives Rs 90/hour, B gives Rs 120/hour — satisfy B's demand first, then allocate remaining hours to A.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Limiting Factor (Throughput) Analysis
frameworks.definition: Identification of the binding constraint on output and measurement of throughput (sales minus truly variable cost) per unit of that constraint to guide short-term decisions.
frameworks.purpose: To focus improvement and product decisions on the constraint that actually limits profit.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Bottleneck management; product ranking; investment in de-bottlenecking.
frameworks.required_inputs: Process capacities, truly variable costs, selling prices, demand.
frameworks.limitations: Constraints shift once relieved; assumes short-term stability; needs accurate capacity data.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Optimising non-constraints; treating labour as variable when it is effectively fixed in the short term.
frameworks.example: Throughput per bottleneck hour identifies which product to prioritise and what an extra bottleneck hour is worth — capping de-bottlenecking spend.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Pricing Strategy Framework
frameworks.definition: A structured choice between pricing approaches — cost-plus, target costing, marginal-cost pricing, market-based and value-based pricing — matched to objectives, costs, demand and competition.
frameworks.purpose: To set prices that cover costs, reflect value and remain competitive, rather than defaulting to a single rule.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: New product launches, tender pricing, special orders, regulated or competitive markets.
frameworks.required_inputs: Cost structure, demand elasticity evidence, competitor prices, customer value perceptions, capacity.
frameworks.limitations: Demand estimates are uncertain; cost-plus ignores the market; value-based pricing needs customer insight.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Cost-plus pricing in a competitive market; pricing below incremental cost; ignoring the signal a price sends about quality.
frameworks.example: A new SaaS product uses value-based pricing against the customer's payroll-processing cost, not its own near-zero marginal cost.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Capital Investment Appraisal Techniques
frameworks.definition: The syllabus set of investment appraisal techniques: NPV, APV, IRR, MIRR, EIRR, payback, capital rationing, profitability index, scenario planning, replacement analysis and sensitivity analysis.
frameworks.purpose: To evaluate capital projects consistently — ranking, accept/reject, and rationing decisions — with risk explicitly addressed.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: New projects, expansions, replacements, acquisitions; capital rationing under funding constraints.
frameworks.required_inputs: Incremental cash flows, discount rate (WACC or risk-adjusted), project life, tax and working capital effects, key risk variables.
frameworks.limitations: Garbage in, garbage out — cash flow forecasts dominate; single discount rate for multi-risk projects; strategic value hard to capture.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Appraising accounting profit instead of cash flow; ignoring working capital and tax; using IRR to rank mutually exclusive projects of different scale.
frameworks.example: A Rs 50m plant: NPV positive at 14% WACC, IRR 19%, payback 3.2 years — but sensitivity shows NPV turns negative if sales fall 15%, so the sales forecast is the decision variable.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Net Present Value (NPV)
frameworks.definition: The sum of discounted incremental cash flows of a project minus the initial investment, discounted at the opportunity cost of capital. Accept if NPV > 0.
frameworks.purpose: The primary investment decision rule — measures absolute value creation in today's money.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: All capital investment decisions; mutually exclusive project choice; valuation of cash-generating assets.
frameworks.required_inputs: Incremental after-tax cash flows by year, discount rate, initial outlay, terminal value if any.
frameworks.limitations: Sensitive to the discount rate and long-horizon forecasts; does not capture managerial flexibility (real options).
frameworks.common_mistakes: Including financing flows or interest in operating cash flows (double-counting the discount rate); inconsistent nominal/real treatment; ignoring working capital.
frameworks.example: Outlay Rs 100m; inflows Rs 30m p.a. for 5 years at 12%: PV of annuity Rs 108.1m, NPV Rs 8.1m — accept.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Internal Rate of Return (IRR)
frameworks.definition: The discount rate at which a project's NPV equals zero; compared against the cost of capital (accept if IRR exceeds it).
frameworks.purpose: A relative return measure useful for communicating project attractiveness and for capital rationing alongside NPV.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Project screening; comparing returns to hurdle rates; situations where percentage returns aid communication.
frameworks.limitations: Multiple IRRs with non-conventional cash flows; reinvestment assumed at the IRR itself; can misrank mutually exclusive projects of different scale or timing.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Ranking mutually exclusive projects by IRR alone; ignoring the multiple-IRR problem; treating IRR as value created.
frameworks.example: A project's IRR of 19% exceeds the 14% WACC, supporting acceptance — but NPV remains the tie-breaker against a smaller, higher-IRR alternative.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Payback Period
frameworks.definition: The time required for cumulative cash inflows to recover the initial investment; shorter is preferred against a target payback.
frameworks.purpose: A simple liquidity and risk screen — how quickly capital is recovered — used alongside discounted methods, never alone for the decision.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Quick screening; high-uncertainty environments; liquidity-constrained firms.
frameworks.required_inputs: Initial investment, annual (or cumulative) cash inflows.
frameworks.limitations: Ignores the time value of money and all cash flows after payback; biased against long-life strategic projects.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using payback as the sole decision rule; using accounting profit instead of cash flow.
frameworks.example: Rs 100m outlay, Rs 35m annual inflow → payback 2.86 years, inside a 3-year policy limit — but NPV must still be checked.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Discounted Payback Period
frameworks.definition: The payback period computed on discounted cash flows — the time until cumulative present values recover the initial investment.
frameworks.purpose: A payback measure that respects the time value of money, useful as a risk/liquidity complement to NPV.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Risk screening of long-life projects; communicating recovery time in present-value terms.
frameworks.required_inputs: Initial investment, cash inflows by year, discount rate.
frameworks.limitations: Still ignores post-payback cash flows; adds little beyond NPV for the accept/reject decision.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Treating it as a substitute for NPV rather than a complement.
frameworks.example: Discounted payback of 3.4 years vs simple payback of 2.9 years shows the true time cost of capital recovery.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Adjusted Present Value (APV)
frameworks.definition: APV values a project as: base-case NPV (as if all-equity financed) plus the present value of financing side effects (e.g. tax shield on debt, issue costs, subsidies).
frameworks.purpose: To appraise projects where financing is complex, changing, or project-specific — common in acquisitions and leveraged deals.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Leveraged acquisitions; projects with subsidised or changing debt levels; demergers and spin-outs.
frameworks.required_inputs: Unlevered cash flows, unlevered (asset) discount rate, debt schedule, tax rate, financing costs.
frameworks.limitations: More complex and assumption-heavy; the unlevered rate must be estimated carefully; financing effects must not be double-counted.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Discounting the tax shield at the wrong rate without justification; mixing APV with WACC-based NPV on the same flows.
frameworks.example: Base NPV Rs 12m plus PV of tax shield Rs 5m less issue costs Rs 1m gives APV Rs 16m for a leveraged buyout target.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC)
frameworks.definition: The blended cost of a firm's capital: the market-value-weighted average of the cost of equity and the after-tax cost of debt (and other capital), used as the discount rate for firm-level appraisals.
frameworks.purpose: To set the hurdle rate for investment appraisal and the discount rate for firm valuations.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Project appraisal; business valuation; capital structure decisions; impairment testing discount rates.
frameworks.required_inputs: Cost of equity (CAPM or dividend model), after-tax cost of debt, market values of equity and debt, tax rate.
frameworks.limitations: Assumes constant capital structure and risk; book values mislead — use market values; a single WACC misprices projects of different risk.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using book weights instead of market weights; forgetting the tax shield on debt; using the firm's WACC for a project of very different risk.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM)
frameworks.definition: CAPM prices systematic risk: expected return = risk-free rate + beta × (expected market return − risk-free rate). Beta measures sensitivity to market (systematic) risk; the security market line (SML) identifies under- and over-valued securities.
frameworks.purpose: To estimate the cost of equity, analyse sensitivity to systematic risk, and judge whether securities are mispriced relative to the SML.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Cost of equity estimation; ungearing and re-gearing beta for different capital structures; investment appraisal of listed securities.
frameworks.required_inputs: Risk-free rate, expected market return (or market risk premium), equity beta (ungeared/re-geared as needed).
frameworks.limitations: Single-factor and backward-looking betas; assumes efficient markets and stable relationships; market portfolio is unobservable.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Using a historical beta without judgement; mismatching nominal/real inputs; applying a levered beta to an unlevered project.
frameworks.example: Rf 10%, market return 16%, beta 1.2 → cost of equity 17.2%. A share offering 15% expected return at beta 1.2 plots below the SML — overvalued.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Financing Choice Framework
frameworks.definition: A structured evaluation of funding options — debt, equity, Islamic finance modes, retained earnings — on quantitative (cost, dilution, covenants, flexibility) and qualitative (control, signalling, Shariah compliance, availability) criteria.
frameworks.purpose: To recommend the most suitable financing mix for a given need, balancing cost, risk, control and feasibility.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Expansion funding, refinancing, start-up capital, rights issues, sukuk vs conventional debt.
frameworks.required_inputs: Funding amount and timing, current capital structure, cost estimates per source, covenant terms, shareholder objectives.
frameworks.limitations: Market access assumptions may not hold (especially for smaller firms); qualitative factors resist scoring.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Choosing purely on headline cost while ignoring covenants, dilution and control; ignoring Islamic finance options where relevant.
frameworks.example: A family firm needing Rs 200m: debt is cheaper post-tax but covenants restrict dividends the family relies on — a phased mix of term finance and retained earnings is recommended.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Risk-Return Trade-off Analysis
frameworks.definition: Analysis of the relationship between risk (systematic vs unsystematic/diversifiable risk) and expected return, including how diversification reduces unsystematic risk.
frameworks.purpose: To ensure return targets are judged against the risk taken and to explain why diversification matters.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Portfolio construction context; explaining required returns; risk-adjusted performance discussion.
frameworks.required_inputs: Expected returns, risk measures (beta, standard deviation), correlations between assets.
frameworks.limitations: Historical risk may not repeat; single-period lens; does not capture liquidity or tail risk.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Comparing returns without adjusting for risk; assuming diversification eliminates all risk (systematic risk remains).
frameworks.example: Two funds return 14%: fund A with beta 1.4 has taken far more systematic risk than fund B with beta 0.9 — B is the better risk-adjusted choice.
frameworks.source_ref: Supplementary business framework — examinability not verified for current ICAP syllabus

frameworks.name: Sensitivity Analysis
frameworks.definition: A technique that varies one key input at a time to measure its effect on the outcome (e.g. NPV), identifying which assumptions the decision is most sensitive to and the breakeven value of each variable.
frameworks.purpose: To focus management attention and further investigation on the assumptions that actually drive the decision.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Every investment appraisal and valuation; budget risk review; any model-based recommendation.
frameworks.required_inputs: Base-case model, list of key variables, plausible ranges for each.
frameworks.limitations: One variable at a time — ignores correlations between variables; does not give probabilities.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Varying variables by arbitrary percentages instead of plausible ranges; not computing the breakeven (switching) value; presenting sensitivity with no conclusion.
frameworks.example: NPV is positive in the base case but turns negative if selling price falls 6% — price is the critical variable; the recommendation is conditional on price protection.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Scenario Planning and Analysis
frameworks.definition: Evaluation of outcomes under a small set of coherent, plausible futures (e.g. base, optimistic, pessimistic) with internally consistent assumptions, often with probabilities or expected values.
frameworks.purpose: To test robustness of a decision across futures and to prepare contingent responses, rather than betting on a single forecast.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Strategic investments; valuations under uncertainty; stress-testing budgets and financing plans.
frameworks.required_inputs: Key uncertainties, coherent scenario narratives, quantified assumptions per scenario, decision triggers.
frameworks.limitations: Scenarios are judgemental; a few scenarios cannot cover all futures; false precision if probabilities are guessed.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Scenarios that are just best/worst tweaks of one variable (that is sensitivity, not scenario); no action linked to each scenario.
frameworks.example: Plant expansion: base case NPV Rs 40m; recession scenario NPV −Rs 25m with 30% probability — expected NPV still positive, but phase the investment with a review trigger.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Enterprise Value vs Equity Value
frameworks.definition: The valuation bridge: enterprise value (value of the whole firm to all capital providers) and equity value (value to shareholders), linked by net debt and non-operating items; underpins DCF, multiple and asset-based appraisals.
frameworks.purpose: To keep valuations consistent — matching the right cash flows to the right value (firm vs equity) and the right discount rate.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Business valuations, M&A pricing, rights issues, capital structure analysis.
frameworks.required_inputs: Forecast free cash flows (to firm or to equity), WACC or cost of equity, net debt, non-operating assets.
frameworks.limitations: Bridge items (pensions, leases, minorities) are often mismeasured; market values of debt may be unavailable.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Discounting free cash flow to firm at the cost of equity; subtracting book debt instead of market net debt; double-counting cash.
frameworks.example: DCF gives enterprise value Rs 900m; less net debt Rs 300m gives equity value Rs 600m — the per-share price follows from shares outstanding.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Business Valuation Techniques
frameworks.definition: The syllabus valuation toolkit: dividend-based models (dividend yield, dividend discount/Gordon model), price-earnings multiples, discounted cash flow valuation, and asset-based valuations.
frameworks.purpose: To estimate business or share value for investment, acquisition, disposal and reporting decisions, triangulating across methods.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Acquisitions and disposals, investment appraisal of shares, shareholder value analysis, dispute and reporting valuations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Dividend history and policy, earnings, forecast cash flows, discount rates, comparable multiples, asset values.
frameworks.limitations: Each method has blind spots — multiples embed market mood, DCF embeds forecasts, asset bases ignore intangibles; triangulation is essential.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Relying on a single method; using unadjusted multiples from incomparable firms; valuing with inconsistent growth assumptions across methods.
frameworks.example: Target valued at Rs 420m (DCF), Rs 460m (P/E multiple), Rs 380m (net assets) — triangulated range Rs 400–450m guides the bid.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Portfolio Selection Theory
frameworks.definition: The theory of optimal portfolio selection: diversifiable (unsystematic) vs non-diversifiable (systematic) risk; correlation and covariance; two-, three- and multiple-asset portfolios and the diversification benefit.
frameworks.purpose: To construct portfolios that maximise expected return for a given risk (or minimise risk for a target return).
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Investment portfolio appraisal; explaining diversification benefits; risk analysis of asset combinations.
frameworks.required_inputs: Expected returns, standard deviations, pairwise correlations/covariances, investment constraints.
frameworks.limitations: Inputs are estimated from history; assumes rational mean-variance investors; correlations spike in crises.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Adding assets without checking correlation (no diversification if perfectly correlated); confusing total risk with systematic risk.
frameworks.example: Combining two assets with correlation 0.2 cuts portfolio standard deviation well below the weighted average — the diversification gain is quantified via covariance.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Hedging Financial Risks
frameworks.definition: The syllabus hedging toolkit: interest-rate hedging (futures, options, swaps, swaptions, forward agreements); foreign-exchange hedging (currency futures, swaps, options, forwards, swaptions, money market hedge); commodity and security forwards and futures.
frameworks.purpose: To reduce the volatility of cash flows and profits arising from interest rate, currency and commodity price movements.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Exporters/importers with FX exposure; borrowers facing rate rises; commodity price exposure.
frameworks.required_inputs: Exposure amounts and timing, market prices of hedging instruments, basis and margin requirements.
frameworks.limitations: Hedging has a cost and can cap upside; basis risk means hedges are imperfect; over-hedging creates new exposure.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Hedging without measuring the exposure first; ignoring the cost-benefit of the hedge; speculating disguised as hedging.
frameworks.example: An exporter expecting USD 2m in 90 days locks the rate with a forward contract, removing FX uncertainty from the quarter's cash forecast.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CAF-6 and CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge References

frameworks.name: Liquidity Risk Management
frameworks.definition: Managing the risk of being unable to meet short-term obligations: liquidity indicators, stress testing, cash forecasting and contingency funding planning.
frameworks.purpose: To ensure survival — that obligations can be met under both normal and stressed conditions.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Treasury reviews; going-concern assessments; growth funding; covenant compliance.
frameworks.required_inputs: Cash flow forecasts, maturity profiles, undrawn facilities, liquid asset buffers, covenant terms.
frameworks.limitations: Forecasts are uncertain; indicators are backward-looking; contingency lines may be withdrawn in stress.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Relying on a single ratio; no stressed forecast; assuming facilities will always be renewed.
frameworks.example: Stress test: a 20% sales delay breaches the current ratio covenant in month 4 — contingency is a pre-agreed facility increase, not hope.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

frameworks.name: Credit Risk Management
frameworks.definition: Managing the risk of customer or counterparty default through financial and non-financial analysis of creditworthiness, credit limits and terms, factoring, and credit insurance.
frameworks.purpose: To protect cash flow and profits from bad debts while supporting profitable sales.
frameworks.appropriate_situations: Credit policy design; major customer exposure reviews; export credit decisions.
frameworks.required_inputs: Customer financials, payment history, credit agency reports, collateral, insurance terms, factoring costs.
frameworks.limitations: Analysis is backward-looking; concentration risk can build silently; insurance and factoring have costs and exclusions.
frameworks.common_mistakes: Extending credit to win sales without limit reviews; no monitoring after the initial approval; ignoring country risk on exports.
frameworks.example: A distributor's largest customer takes 40% of sales with deteriorating ratios — response: reduce the limit, require partial advance, and insure the balance.
frameworks.source_ref: ICAP Directive 1.01 (Revised 2024), CFAP-4 Specific Examinable Knowledge Reference

framework_steps.title: Gather internal evidence
framework_steps.description: Collect financials, operational data and capability assessments to evidence Strengths and Weaknesses.

framework_steps.title: Scan the external environment
framework_steps.description: Identify Opportunities and Threats from market, competitor, regulatory and economic analysis.

framework_steps.title: Build the matrix
framework_steps.description: Place each evidenced factor in the correct quadrant; keep internal and external strictly separate.

framework_steps.title: Generate TOWS strategies
framework_steps.description: Match quadrants: use Strengths to capture Opportunities (SO), fix Weaknesses to pursue Opportunities (WO), use Strengths against Threats (ST), minimise Weaknesses and avoid Threats (WT).

framework_steps.title: Prioritise and conclude
framework_steps.description: Rank factors by impact and likelihood; state the 2–3 strategic implications that follow.

framework_steps.title: Define scope
framework_steps.description: Fix the market, geography and time horizon the scan covers.

framework_steps.title: Identify factors per heading
framework_steps.description: List Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal factors with evidence, not assertion.

framework_steps.title: Assess impact and likelihood
framework_steps.description: Rate each factor's likely impact on the business and its probability over the horizon.

framework_steps.title: Convert to opportunities and threats
framework_steps.description: Translate the highest-rated factors into specific opportunities and threats for strategy and risk work.

framework_steps.title: Define the industry
framework_steps.description: Set clear industry boundaries (product and geography) — the forces depend on this definition.

framework_steps.title: Assess each force
framework_steps.description: Rate threat of new entrants, supplier power, buyer power, substitute threat and rivalry as strong, moderate or weak, with evidence for each.

framework_steps.title: Judge overall attractiveness
framework_steps.description: Combine the five assessments into an overall verdict on industry profit potential.

framework_steps.title: Draw strategic implications
framework_steps.description: Identify where the firm can defend, differentiate or reshape the forces (e.g. raise switching costs).

framework_steps.title: Define units and markets
framework_steps.description: Split the portfolio into strategic business units and define each unit's market.

framework_steps.title: Compute positions
framework_steps.description: Calculate relative market share (unit share ÷ largest competitor share) and market growth rate per unit.
framework_steps.formula: Relative share = own share / largest competitor share

framework_steps.title: Plot and classify
framework_steps.description: Place each unit as Star, Cash Cow, Question Mark or Dog.

framework_steps.title: Set portfolio strategy
framework_steps.description: Allocate: invest in Stars, harvest Cash Cows, selectively fund Question Marks, divest or fix Dogs — checking cash balance across the portfolio.

framework_steps.title: Map activities
framework_steps.description: List primary and support activities for the business.

framework_steps.title: Assign costs and value
framework_steps.description: Attribute costs to activities and assess each activity's contribution to customer value and margin.

framework_steps.title: Analyse linkages
framework_steps.description: Examine how activities connect — where coordination creates or destroys value.

framework_steps.title: Target advantage
framework_steps.description: Recommend cost or differentiation moves at the activities with the greatest value leverage.

framework_steps.title: Clean the data
framework_steps.description: Adjust for one-offs, policy changes and window-dressing; use averages for balance-sheet items where appropriate.

framework_steps.title: Compute ratio families
framework_steps.description: Calculate profitability, liquidity, efficiency, gearing and investor ratios for 2–3 years.

framework_steps.title: Trend and benchmark
framework_steps.description: Compare over time and against industry peers to separate firm-specific from sector-wide movements.

framework_steps.title: Interpret and investigate
framework_steps.description: Explain what the ratios signal, cross-check with the cash flow statement, and list follow-up questions.

framework_steps.title: Split costs
framework_steps.description: Separate fixed and variable costs; identify stepped costs near capacity.

framework_steps.title: Compute contribution
framework_steps.description: Contribution per unit = selling price − variable cost per unit; contribution margin ratio = contribution ÷ sales.
framework_steps.formula: Breakeven (units) = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit

framework_steps.title: Find breakeven and margin of safety
framework_steps.description: Breakeven revenue = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin ratio; margin of safety = (forecast − breakeven) ÷ forecast.
framework_steps.formula: Margin of safety = (Forecast sales − Breakeven sales) / Forecast sales

framework_steps.title: Stress-test
framework_steps.description: Recompute for price, cost and volume changes; state what volume or price the plan depends on.

framework_steps.title: Identify incremental cash flows
framework_steps.description: Forecast after-tax operating cash flows, working capital movements and terminal value — cash, not profit.

framework_steps.title: Set the discount rate
framework_steps.description: Use WACC (or a risk-adjusted rate); keep nominal/real consistent with the cash flows.

framework_steps.title: Discount and sum
framework_steps.description: Discount each year's cash flow and the initial outlay to present value; NPV = PV of inflows − initial investment.

framework_steps.title: Decide and stress-test
framework_steps.description: Accept if NPV > 0; run sensitivity on the key variables before finalising.

framework_steps.title: Estimate cost of equity
framework_steps.description: Use CAPM (or dividend/growth models); ungear and re-gear beta if leverage differs.

framework_steps.title: Estimate after-tax cost of debt
framework_steps.description: Use yield to maturity (or effective interest cost); multiply by (1 − tax rate).

framework_steps.title: Weight by market values
framework_steps.description: WACC = (E/V)×Ke + (D/V)×Kd(after tax) using market, not book, values.

framework_steps.title: Sense-check
framework_steps.description: Confirm the capital structure is stable and the rate suits the project's risk; adjust for project-specific risk if needed.

framework_steps.title: Get the risk-free rate
framework_steps.description: Use a government security yield matching the horizon, in the same nominal/real terms as the analysis.

framework_steps.title: Estimate beta
framework_steps.description: Use an equity beta; ungear (remove leverage) and re-gear for the target capital structure where needed.

framework_steps.title: Apply the SML
framework_steps.description: Expected return = Rf + β(market risk premium); compare actual expected returns to the SML to spot mispricing.

framework_steps.title: Build the base case
framework_steps.description: Finalise the base-case model and decision metric (NPV, profit, etc.).

framework_steps.title: Select key variables
framework_steps.description: Choose the inputs with the greatest uncertainty and impact (price, volume, costs, discount rate).

framework_steps.title: Vary one at a time
framework_steps.description: Change each variable across its plausible range, holding others constant; record the metric's response.

framework_steps.title: Find switching values
framework_steps.description: Compute the breakeven value of each variable where the decision flips; rank variables by sensitivity.

framework_steps.title: Identify key uncertainties
framework_steps.description: List the 2–3 uncertainties that most affect the decision.

framework_steps.title: Build coherent scenarios
framework_steps.description: Write base, upside and downside narratives with internally consistent assumptions (not single-variable tweaks).

framework_steps.title: Quantify each scenario
framework_steps.description: Run the model under each scenario; compute expected value if probabilities can be justified.

framework_steps.title: Decide with contingencies
framework_steps.description: Choose the robust option and attach trigger-based actions per scenario.

framework_steps.title: Choose methods
framework_steps.description: Select at least two of DCF, dividend models, P/E multiples and asset-based approaches suited to the firm.

framework_steps.title: Value under each method
framework_steps.description: Apply consistent growth and risk assumptions across methods.

framework_steps.title: Bridge EV to equity
framework_steps.description: Adjust enterprise values for net debt and non-operating items to reach equity value per share.
framework_steps.formula: Equity value = Enterprise value − Net debt ± non-operating items

framework_steps.title: Triangulate
framework_steps.description: Reconcile the range across methods; explain differences; state a valuation range, not a false point estimate.

framework_steps.title: Measure the exposure
framework_steps.description: Quantify the FX, interest-rate or commodity exposure by amount and timing.

framework_steps.title: Set the hedging objective
framework_steps.description: Decide what to protect (cash flow certainty vs cost minimisation) and the hedge ratio.

framework_steps.title: Select instruments
framework_steps.description: Choose from forwards, futures, options, swaps, swaptions or money-market hedges based on cost, flexibility and availability.

framework_steps.title: Compare cost vs benefit
framework_steps.description: Weigh the hedge cost and any upside given up against the volatility removed; avoid over-hedging.

framework_steps.title: Measure the cycle
framework_steps.description: Compute inventory days, receivable days and payable days, and the cash conversion cycle.
framework_steps.formula: CCC = Inventory days + Receivable days − Payable days

framework_steps.title: Diagnose the drivers
framework_steps.description: Identify which component drives the cycle and why (policy, process, customer/supplier power).

framework_steps.title: Set target policies
framework_steps.description: Set credit, inventory and payment policies balancing cash release against sales and supply risk.

framework_steps.title: Quantify and monitor
framework_steps.description: Quantify the cash released and financing saved; monitor the cycle monthly against targets.
